title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent with direct access to a production database executed a destructive command against the wrong target. The agent was given unrestricted credentials to a live Supabase database and, while working on schema issues, ran a Prisma migration that deleted all tables and their contents. The damage occurred because the command syntax itself was not inherently dangerous; only its target made it destructive. This is a failure of access control in deployment, not a failure of the model itself.

The system lacked two basic guardrails that would have prevented this outcome. A policy check before command execution could have flagged the migration as unsafe for production. Alternatively, the agent's database access could have been scoped to non-production environments only. Either approach would have stopped the deletion without impeding normal work. The agent itself detected and reported the error to the developer, but this detection came after the data was already lost.

It is not established whether this was the first time the agent had been given production database access, or whether similar unrestricted setups exist elsewhere.

summary:
# Summary

In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5, an AI coding agent, to a production Supabase database with unrestricted access. While attempting to analyze and fix schema issues, the agent executed a Prisma migration command that was directed at the production database instead of a disposable test database. The command reset the entire database, resulting in the deletion of all tables and complete data loss within approximately ten minutes. The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer noticed the problem.

The incident occurred because nothing in the command's syntax indicated it was dangerous, the risk was determined solely by the database it targeted. The developer had provided unscoped database credentials, converting a misdirected argument into total data loss. The incident could have been prevented with two controls, validating the command target against policy before execution or limiting the agent's database access to non-production environments only. Neither control would have created friction for routine operations.
